Mask data represent **regions** in each frame rather than single coordinates.

## How Mask Data Is Represented

In Neuralyzer, a mask is represented as a **binary spatial region** for a given frame/time index:

- Pixels inside the object are foreground.
- Pixels outside the object are background.
- A feature can have different mask geometry at different times.

This makes masks suitable when full object shape matters (for example tongue/body outlines, contact patches, segmented structures), not just point locations.

## How Masks Appear in the Media Viewer

When a mask feature is enabled, the Media Viewer draws it as a semi-transparent overlay on top of the media.

- **Color and alpha** control visibility and contrast against the image/video.
- Multiple mask features can be viewed together for comparison.
- The rendered overlay is display-focused; exported data keeps the mask geometry representation.

## Temporal Behavior

Masks are frame-aware and TimeFrame-aware:

- At each current frame, the viewer displays the corresponding mask sample.
- If no mask exists at a frame, nothing is drawn for that feature at that time.
- TimeFrame assignment controls synchronization with other modalities.

## Practical Tip

Use masks when your downstream analysis depends on **shape**, **coverage**, or **boundary geometry**. Use points when you only need one tracked location.
